note: Mitchell's 'algeria' agricultural series (crop areas/production, 1902-1918) shows the same civil-departments-vs-full-colony reporting gap already documented here for IIA (issue 166): the data's cropland magnitudes are plausible only for northern Algeria (Alger/Oran/Constantine), not the Sahara included in this polity's polygon. This corroborates that the gap is a property of French colonial agricultural statistics generally, not specific to the IIA yearbooks, but does not resolve oq-dza-civil-departments-as-a-reporting-unit since no separate polygon/polity exists to route it to.

Neither the page nor the assertion bundle addresses whether Mitchell's 'India' production series for 1937-1946 include output from the princely states (nominally under British paramountcy but not administratively absorbed, and included in the row's polygon) or cover British-administered provinces only. Pre-1947 Indian colonial agricultural statistics are frequently province-based and may under-cover princely-state production; this is a potential sub-territory fold-up worth flagging for future review if finer provenance on Mitchell's underlying colonial-yearbook sources becomes available, though the observed magnitudes are not obviously inconsistent with either scope.

The Chaco War (1932-1935), during which Paraguay occupied most of the disputed Gran Chaco, falls inside this polity's own observed data span (1910-1937) even though formal cession only came with the 1938 treaty — the page currently frames the war only as the reason for the 1938 predecessor/successor split, not as a mid-span territorial-control event that bears on how agricultural statistics for the disputed region may have been (or not been) reported during 1932-1935.

The DB carries American Samoa as a separate polity (ASM-1900-2025, 197 km2 per biger-1995's own american-samoa entry, p.30), which the page does not mention. This rules out the "combined Samoa" failure mode explicitly: IIA's "samoa" cacao-beans series (German-plantation-era crop) plausibly belongs to Western Samoa only, not the tiny US-administered eastern islands.

The page is silent on the Portuguese colonial period's economy and on IIA-sourced data; for the record, IIA yearbooks report coffee (green, median ~1,050 t/yr) and cacao (beans, median ~10 t/yr) for Portuguese Timor across 1909-1940, a period during which the Portuguese/Dutch Timor boundary (fixed 1904, arbitrated by the Permanent Court of Arbitration in 1914) was stable, so this label safely maps to the same territory as today's Timor-Leste minus no relevant change in that span.
